item.title: APA offers new guidance as artificial intelligence use at work expands
item.description:
# APA offers new guidance as artificial intelligence use at work expands - [AI and Chatbots](https://www.apa.org/topics/artificial-intelligence-machine-learning)
_Seven research-based practices offer steps for evaluating and introducing AI tools with a focus on trust, human oversight, job design and workers’ well-being_
_APA offers new guidance as artificial intelligence use at work expands_ [Press release]. [https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2026/11/artificial-intelligence-work-guidance](https://www.apa.org/news/press/releases/2026/11/artificial-intelligence-work-guidance)
Washington — As organizations introduce artificial intelligence (AI) tools to their workforce, people may be left to navigate unclear policies, conflicting expectations and new questions about trust and acceptable AI use in the workplace.
Created for organizations seeking to adopt AI responsibly while also supporting employees and improving how work is designed, [_Deploying AI Into Workplaces: What Leaders Need to Know_](https://www.apa.org/pubs/reports/ai-workforce) offers seven best practices based on established psychological research and emerging evidence about AI. These range from matching safeguards to the stakes of potential errors to ensuring that AI is introduced through a fair process.
“The rapidly growing use of AI at work is creating new behaviors and social judgments while raising questions about trust, all of which are fundamentally questions of psychology. APA’s new guide gives leaders a practical framework for introducing AI thoughtfully, with people at the center of the process.”
It also offers examples of what effective AI tool implementation can look like, as well as identifies the red flags to watch out for.
- ensuring that AI is introduced through a fair process, including consulting with those who will be using the new system and those who will be affected by the outputs of that system; and - protecting opportunities for people to develop deep expertise, share knowledge and learn from experience.
That means giving workers the information they need to judge where AI tools are reliable and where they are not, making sure human oversight is meaningful and rethinking how jobs are designed.”

item.title: DOE Explains...Artificial Intelligence
item.description:
# DOE Explains...Artificial Intelligence ![Supercomputers like the Department of Energy’s Aurora at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility will help make artificial intelligence more and more powerful.](https://www.energy.gov/sites/default/files/styles/full_article_width/public/2024-07/doe-explains-artificial-intelligence.jpg?itok=zZ0wBGLD)
Supercomputers like the Department of Energy’s Aurora at the Argonne Leadership Computing Facility will help make artificial intelligence more and more powerful.
Image courtesy of Argonne Leadership Computing Facility
**Artificial Intelligence (AI)** simply means intelligence in machines, in contrast to natural intelligence found in humans and other natural organisms. Artificial intelligence gained its name and became a formal field of research in 1956, and initial work led to new tools for solving mathematical problems. However, researchers discovered that creating an AI is incredibly difficult, and progress slowed in the 1970s. More recently, increases in computing power and availability of massive data sets have set the groundwork for advances in AI.
In particular, scientists have made giant strides in one particular application of AI, [machine learning](https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsmachine-learning). Machine learning involves systems that automatically learn from the data they analyze and the results they obtain to improve their ability to work with that data in the future. For example, machine learning powers applications that estimate how long a trip will take and then provide guidance on the route. Applications such as Google Maps use machine learning to analyze shifting traffic conditions and incorporate user-reported data to reduce travel times and suggest fuel-efficient routes. Machine learning is best for these types of specific, well-defined tasks that can be broken down into logical steps.
The next level of AI application is known as **deep learning**. Deep learning involves complex tasks with many hard to nail down variables. It makes use of neural networks, which seek to build computers that operate like our brains. Deep learning leverages many neural networks stacked on top of each other to create a large, complex neural network. Deep learning demands a lot of computing power to both train the model from copious amounts of data and use the trained models to make decisions. One example is digital assistants like Amazon Alexa, Apple Siri, and Google Assistant. Deep learning is what allows these assistants to listen to you and figure out what information you want or task you need them to perform.
## DOE Office of Science: Contributions to Artificial Intelligence The Advanced Scientific Computing Research (ASCR) program in the Department of Energy Office of Science (DOE SC) has been working on AI since the 1960s. ASCR developed several technologies--including massively parallel input/output systems and linear algebra routines--that led to today’s AI systems. More recently, ASCR’s role in high-performance computing and exascale computing will help build the hardware and software needed to power future generations of AI. The ASCR program also provides support to other DOE SC programs that are using AI to accomplish their goals. For example, the DOE SC Fusion Energy Science program is deploying AI to help control fusion reactions with the goal of making [fusion energy](https://www.energy.gov/science/doe-explainsfusion-energy-science) production a commercial reality.
## Artificial Intelligence Facts One of the ways we can understand advances in AI is how well it performs at games.
- In 2011, [IBM’s Watson(link is external)](https://community.ibm.com/community/user/storage/blogs/tony-pearson1/2021/02/18/ibm-watson-plays-jeopardy-ten-years-later?mhsrc=ibmsearch_a&mhq=watson%20jeopardy) won the U.S. game show Jeopardy! - In 2016, the [Google DeepMind AlphaGo(link is external)](https://deepmind.com/research/case-studies/alphago-the-story-so-far) AI beat a human grandmaster at the complex Chinese game of Go. - But humans say AI [isn’t so good at games involving teamwork(link is external)](https://news.mit.edu/2021/does-artificial-intelligence-play-well-others-1004).
## Resources and Related Terms _It also describes how these concepts apply to the work that the Department of Energy’s Office of Science conducts as it helps the United States excel in research across the scientific spectrum._

item.title: Human Intelligence Meets Artificial Intelligence: Why the Future of Journalism Belongs to Those Who Master Both
item.description:
TMF Executive Director, Dastan Kamanzi challenged journalists to reconsider their perceptions of artificial intelligence, arguing that the technology should be viewed as an opportunity rather than an automatic threat to their professional survival.
As artificial intelligence (AI) increasingly finds its way into newsrooms, journalists around the world are confronting an uncomfortable question: Is technology gradually taking over the profession, or is it creating an opportunity to redefine journalism and make it more impactful?
For journalists who fear that machines could eventually replace their jobs, the message from [Tanzania Media Foundation](https://gfmd.info/members/tanzania-media-foundation/) (TMF) is that the future may not belong to artificial intelligence alone, but to professionals who understand how to combine machine capabilities with human intelligence.
Facilitating the session, TMF Executive Director, Dastan Kamanzi challenged journalists to reconsider their perceptions of artificial intelligence, arguing that the technology should be viewed as an opportunity rather than an automatic threat to their professional survival.
“People should not be worried simply because Artificial Intelligence is here and might take their jobs.
Artificial intelligence, meanwhile, has considerable strengths in processing large volumes of information, identifying patterns, recognising relationships in datasets, automating repetitive tasks and generating preliminary content at remarkable speed.
Despite its advantages, AI presents serious challenges that journalists and media organisations cannot afford to underestimate.
AI systems can produce fabricated facts, incorrect statistics, imaginary quotations and references to publications that do not exist.
AI-generated photographs, manipulated videos and cloned voices can make fabricated events appear genuine.
UNESCO’s 2023 handbook, Reporting on Artificial Intelligence, also encourages journalists to go beyond reporting technological developments as business or product stories.
AI can help them investigate more efficiently, process information faster and produce stories in different formats.
As the technology continues to evolve, one principle should remain unchanged: AI may help journalists find, organise and present information, but it is human intelligence, professional judgement and accountability that must determine what deserves to be published.
